title: Count Distinct Elements
directAnswer: Add all elements to a hash set and return its size. Duplicates collapse automatically. O(n) time, O(n) space.

remember.takeaway: Uniqueness counting is a one-liner with a set.
antiSignals: O(1) space mandated — sort then count adjacent diffs

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums`, return how many distinct values it contains.
understanding: Insert everything into a set; the set's size is the number of distinct values.

approaches.name: Hash set size
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Insert every element into a hash **set** and read its size — the set stores each value at most once, so its size is the count of distinct values. O(n) time, O(n) space.

**Why a set collapses duplicates.** Re-inserting a value already present is a no-op, so after inserting the whole array the set contains exactly the unique values. The answer is just `set.size()` — no manual de-duplication.

**The O(1)-space alternative.** Sort the array, then count positions where an element differs from its predecessor. That's O(n log n) time but O(1) extra space — the classic time-vs-space trade you should name.

**Don't confuse size with length.** Returning `nums.length` counts every element including repeats; you want the *set's* size.

code.python:
def distinct(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    return len(set(nums))

hints: What structure automatically ignores duplicate insertions?
The set's size is your answer — not the array length.
No extra space allowed? Sort and count adjacent changes instead.
approaches.complexityReasoning: each insert is O(1) average, so O(n) time; the set may hold all n values, so O(n) space.
pitfalls: Returning the array length instead of the set size.
Forgetting an empty array has 0 distinct values.

commonMistakes: Counting the array length instead of the set size.
Forgetting that an empty array has 0 distinct values.
